genZNote: P. aeruginosa's much chiller cousin — breaks down pollutants for a living instead of causing hospital outbreaks.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil and water, especially environments with organic/aromatic pollutants
habitat.hostAssociation: Not a normal human commensal; a free-living environmental organism
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Widespread in soil and water; well known for its ability to metabolically degrade aromatic hydrocarbons (toluene, xylene) and other pollutants

culture.growthCharacteristics: Obligate aerobe, grows well at room temperature
culture.pigmentation: May produce fluorescent pigments (fluorescein) under UV light, similar to other fluorescent pseudomonads

identificationClues: Obligate aerobe, motile via polar flagella
Notable for metabolic versatility — degrades aromatic hydrocarbons and other pollutants, used in bioremediation and biotechnology
Generally low virulence compared to P. aeruginosa

diseases: Rarely pathogenic; occasional opportunistic infections (bacteremia, catheter-related infection) almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised or critically ill patients
virulenceFactors: Minimal compared to P. aeruginosa — lacks many of the classic Pseudomonas aeruginosa virulence factors (e.g., exotoxin A, prominent biofilm-mediated device infections are far less common)
clinicalImportance.transmission: Environmental exposure rather than person-to-person spread
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Of far greater biotechnological/environmental importance (bioremediation, industrial biocatalysis) than clinical importance
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: An oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod recovered from a clinical specimen should prompt differentiation from the far more clinically significant P. aeruginosa

examFacts.importantTest: Oxidase test (positive); differentiation from P. aeruginosa by clinical significance and additional biochemical/molecular testing
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: An oxidase-positive environmental Pseudomonas prized for degrading aromatic pollutants, with far lower clinical virulence than P. aeruginosa
